senses.gloss: Every day, continuously and without change, often to the point of boredom.
examples: She rides the same crowded train *day in, day out*.
*Day in, day out*, he answers the same customer complaints.
Farmers work the land *day in, day out*, whatever the weather.

type: viewpoint — in actual practice, whatever the law says
contrast: Much more often an adjective before a noun: *the de facto leader*, *a de facto ban*. Its legal opposite is *de jure* (по закону).

senses.gloss: In fact or in practice, though not officially.
examples: English functions *de facto* as the official language of the United States.
After the governor fell ill, his chief of staff was *de facto* in charge.
The rule was never repealed, but it has been *de facto* abandoned.

senses.gloss: Straight ahead; directly in front.
examples: There's a gas station *dead ahead*.
The captain spotted an iceberg *dead ahead*.
Keep driving and you'll see the lake *dead ahead*.

type: viewpoint — in one's true feelings, beneath the surface

senses.gloss: In one's real feelings or nature, as opposed to how things seem.
examples: *Deep down*, I knew he was right.
She acts tough, but she's a kind person *deep down*.
*Deep down*, everyone wants to be liked.

senses.gloss: At an early stage of something.
examples: I realized *early on* that the job wasn't for me.
*Early on*, the company had only three employees.
Problems like this are easier to fix if you catch them *early on*.

type: manner — all together as a group

senses.gloss: All together, as a large group.
examples: The workers walked out *en masse* to protest the pay cuts.
Fans arrived *en masse* hours before the concert.
The board resigned *en masse* after the scandal.

senses.gloss: On the way to or from a place.
examples: We stopped for lunch *en route* to Denver.
The package is *en route* and should arrive Friday.
The ambulance is already *en route*.

ru: и всё же, тем не менее

senses.gloss: In spite of what was just said.
senses.ru: и всё же, тем не менее
examples: The hotel was a little noisy. *Even so*, we enjoyed our stay.
It's an old car, but *even so*, it runs well.
I know it's risky; *even so*, I want to try.

modifies: adjectives and adverbs, in American English mostly *slightly*, *gently*, *slowly*
contrast: In American English it mostly stresses how small or gentle something is: *ever so slightly*, *ever so gently*. *Thanks ever so* and *ever so nice* sound British.

senses.gloss: Very; to a great degree, often about something small or delicate.
examples: The door opened *ever so* slightly.
She lifted the sleeping baby *ever so* gently.
Things are improving, *ever so* slowly.

ru: ничуть не менее, во всех отношениях
position: before its word — usually in *every bit as … as*
modifies: adjectives and adverbs in *as … as*; a noun phrase (*every bit a leader*)

senses.gloss: In every way; just as much.
senses.ru: ничуть не менее, во всех отношениях
examples: The sequel is *every bit* as good as the original.
She was *every bit* as nervous as I was.
Moving to New York was *every bit* the adventure I'd hoped for.

senses.gloss: Occasionally; not often and not regularly.
examples: *Every now and then*, we order pizza instead of cooking.
I still think about her *every now and then*.
He checks his phone *every now and then* during the meeting.

senses.gloss: Occasionally, at more or less regular intervals.
examples: *Every so often*, a train rumbles past the house.
Stir the soup *every so often* so it doesn't burn.
We meet up for coffee *every so often*.

type: direction — in all directions; also manner: in disorder
contrast: Informal American.

senses.gloss: In all directions.
examples: When the dog ran in, the chickens scattered *every which way*.
Kids were running *every which way* across the playground.

senses.gloss: In a messy, disorderly way.
examples: The books were piled on the shelves *every which way*.
Cars were parked *every which way* after the game.

type: degree — by a very large margin
position: before its word — before a superlative or *the* + noun

senses.gloss: By far; without any doubt.
examples: She is *far and away* the best player on the team.
This was *far and away* the hottest summer on record.
Rent is *far and away* our biggest expense.

senses.gloss: Over a large area; in or from many places.
examples: People came from *far and wide* to hear him speak.
The news spread *far and wide*.
We searched *far and wide* for a good mechanic.

type: manner — in the best class of travel or mail
contrast: As an adverb it takes no article or preposition: *We flew first class*. Before a noun it is an adjective, usually hyphenated: *a first-class ticket*, *first-class service*.

senses.gloss: In the most expensive and comfortable class, or by the fastest regular mail.
examples: The company flew her *first class* to Tokyo.
If I win the lottery, I'm traveling *first class*.
Send the letter *first class* so it gets there by Monday.

type: linking — the first point in a list or argument
contrast: It opens a list of points or firmly states the most basic one. It does not mean *at first* (сначала, поначалу, when things later changed): *At first I hated the job*, not *First of all I hated the job*.

senses.gloss: Before anything else; as the first point.
examples: *First of all*, I want to thank everyone for coming.
*First of all*, you need a valid passport.
Well, *first of all*, I never said that.

senses.gloss: Informal: first; to begin with.
examples: *First off*, let's make sure everyone has a copy.
*First off*, I'm not mad at you.
Okay, *first off*, what time does the store close?

type: manner — bluntly; also degree: at full speed or effort
position: mid or end — before the verb in the *bluntly* sense, after it in the *full speed* sense
modifies: verbs; adjectives in the *bluntly* sense (*flat out wrong*)
contrast: Informal and mainly American. Hyphenated before a noun it is an adjective meaning *complete*: *a flat-out lie*.

senses.gloss: Directly and completely, without softening it.
examples: He *flat out* refused to sign the contract.
She told me *flat out* that she didn't trust me.
That's *flat out* wrong.

senses.gloss: As fast or as hard as possible.
senses.ru: изо всех сил, на полной скорости
examples: We've been working *flat out* to finish before the holidays.
The car was going *flat out* when it hit the wall.

senses.gloss: For very little money.
examples: We bought the old farmhouse *for a song*.
The paintings went *for a song* at the estate sale.
He picked up a used guitar *for a song*.

contrast: *For a while* is a length of time: *I lived there for a while*. *In a while* means *after some time, soon* (через некоторое время): *I'll call you in a while*.

senses.gloss: For a period of time, usually not very long.
examples: Let's sit here *for a while* and rest.
I haven't seen him *for a while*.
She worked in Boston *for a while* before moving home.

contrast: Often misheard and miswritten as *for all intensive purposes*. The British form is *to all intents and purposes*.

senses.gloss: In every practical sense, even if not officially.
examples: *For all intents and purposes*, the deal is done.
The old factory is, *for all intents and purposes*, abandoned.
The election was over *for all intents and purposes* by ten o'clock.

type: viewpoint — in practice, even if not strictly
modifies: a whole clause; an adjective (*for all practical purposes identical*)

senses.gloss: In every way that matters in practice, even if not strictly or officially.
examples: *For all practical purposes*, the two phones are identical.
The town was, *for all practical purposes*, cut off by the flood.
Once they were up by twenty points, the game was over *for all practical purposes*.

position: before its word — before *like*, *as if* or *as though*
contrast: Do not confuse it with *for the world* in negatives: *I wouldn't miss it for the world* = ни за что на свете.

senses.gloss: Exactly; in every way, when something looks or seems like something else.
examples: From across the street, he looked *for all the world* like a movie star.
The recording sounds *for all the world* as if the band were in the room.
She stood there smiling, *for all the world* as though nothing had happened.

contrast: Mostly after *know*, *say* or *tell*, often in negatives and questions: *No one knows for certain*. In everyday speech Americans more often say *for sure*.

senses.gloss: Without any doubt.
examples: Nobody knows *for certain* what caused the fire.
I can't say *for certain* when he'll be back.
Do you know *for certain* that she's coming?

type: degree — as hard as possible, as if one's life depended on it

senses.gloss: As hard or as fast as possible, as if to save one's life.
examples: The little boy held on to the railing *for dear life*.
We ran *for dear life* when the storm hit.
She clung to the edge of the raft *for dear life*.

position: any position — front, mid between commas, or end
modifies: a whole clause or a noun phrase
contrast: *For example* is set off by commas and can move around the sentence; *such as* comes directly before the examples with no comma: *cities such as Boston and Denver*. Abbreviated *e.g.*

senses.gloss: Used to introduce something that shows what you mean.
examples: Many birds, *for example* penguins, cannot fly.
*For example*, you could take the train instead of driving.
Some jobs pay very little. Teaching assistants, *for example*, often earn less than $30,000.

contrast: *Free* alone works too: *Kids eat free*. *For free* is informal but standard in American English. Do not confuse it with *freely* (свободно, открыто).

senses.gloss: Without having to pay.
examples: Kids under five get in *for free*.
I fixed his computer *for free*.
They were giving away T-shirts *for free* at the game.

contrast: *For good* means *forever*, not *for a good reason* or *for the good of*: *He left for good* = он уехал насовсем.

senses.gloss: Permanently; forever.
examples: She moved back to Ohio *for good*.
After the injury, he quit football *for good*.
I think the old diner has closed *for good*.

type: manner — as an extra, beyond what is needed

senses.gloss: As something extra, in addition to what is needed.
examples: He checked the locks twice, and once more *for good measure*.
Add a pinch of salt *for good measure*.
The waiter brought us a free dessert *for good measure*.

modifies: a whole clause or a noun phrase

senses.gloss: As an example.
examples: Some foods, *for instance* peanuts and eggs, often cause allergies.
*For instance*, you could start by walking to work.
Take my brother, *for instance*: he never learned to cook.

contrast: Informal. *Play for keeps* comes from children's games where the winner keeps what is won, so it also means *be completely serious*.

senses.gloss: Informal: permanently, to keep.
examples: You can have the book *for keeps*.
This time, she's leaving the city *for keeps*.
When he said he wanted to win, he was playing *for keeps*.

type: negative — used with a negative: by any means at all
modifies: verbs in negative sentences, usually *can't get* or *couldn't find*

senses.gloss: By any means at all; used only in negative sentences.
examples: You can't get a table there on a Saturday *for love or money*.
I couldn't find a taxi *for love or money*.
He wouldn't sell that truck *for love or money*.

type: focusing — singles out one example, often the speaker
position: after its word — right after a noun or pronoun, between commas
modifies: a noun or pronoun, usually the subject

senses.gloss: As one example of people who think or do something.
examples: I, *for one*, think it's a terrible idea.
Not everyone liked the movie. My wife, *for one*, walked out halfway through.
Plenty of people have doubts: the mayor, *for one*.

senses.gloss: As a shorter form of a name.
examples: His name is Robert, but everyone calls him Bob *for short*.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, or FBI *for short*, opened a case.
It's called the International Space Station, ISS *for short*.

position: end — also alone as a reply

senses.gloss: With certainty.
examples: I don't know *for sure* if the store is open.
We'll know *for sure* after the test results come back.
Nobody can say *for sure* who will win.

senses.gloss: Informal: definitely; used to agree strongly.
examples: 'Are you coming to the party?' '*For sure*!'
That was *for sure* the best meal I've had all year.

ru: если на то пошло, да и вообще
type: linking — adds that the point applies to something else too
modifies: a noun phrase or a whole clause

senses.gloss: Used to say that what is true of one thing is also true of another.
senses.ru: если на то пошло, да и вообще
examples: I don't trust him, or his brother *for that matter*.
She never calls her parents, or anyone else, *for that matter*.
Why would anyone, *for that matter*, want to live there?

senses.gloss: Simply by asking for it, with no other effort or cost.
examples: The job is yours *for the asking*.
Free coffee is available *for the asking* at the front desk.
With his connections, a record deal was his *for the asking*.

type: time — for now, though it may change

senses.gloss: Now, for a short time, though things may change.
examples: *For the moment*, we're staying with my parents.
The rain has stopped *for the moment*.
Let's leave that question aside *for the moment*.

senses.gloss: Mostly; in most cases.
examples: *For the most part*, the students behaved well.
The reviews were, *for the most part*, positive.
I agree with you *for the most part*.

senses.gloss: For now, until something changes.
examples: *For the time being*, the office is closed.
You can use my old laptop *for the time being*.
We're renting an apartment *for the time being*.

contrast: More formal than *for free*; common in notices and ads. *Charge* here means *price*.

senses.gloss: Without any cost.
examples: Delivery is *free of charge* on orders over $50.
The museum is open to the public *free of charge*.
They repaired the phone *free of charge* because it was under warranty.

type: degree — completely, all over the body
modifies: verbs and adjectives describing the body or clothes

senses.gloss: Over the whole body; completely.
examples: The kids came home covered in mud *from head to toe*.
She was dressed in black *from head to toe*.
I was shaking *from head to toe*.

type: manner — from the very beginning, with nothing prepared
contrast: In cooking it means *from basic ingredients, not from a mix*: *She bakes her bread from scratch*.

senses.gloss: From the very beginning, without using anything already done.
examples: The files were lost, so we had to start *from scratch*.
She built the business *from scratch*.
This cake is made *from scratch*, not from a box.

senses.gloss: Through the whole of something, from beginning to end.
examples: The movie was exciting *from start to finish*.
The project took six months *from start to finish*.
She led the race *from start to finish*.

senses.gloss: Sincerely, expressing real feelings.
examples: His speech at the wedding came *from the heart*.
Just speak *from the heart* and you'll be fine.
I mean this *from the heart*: thank you.

senses.gloss: Occasionally; sometimes.
examples: We still see each other *from time to time*.
*From time to time*, the power goes out in our neighborhood.
Check the oil *from time to time*.

position: after its word — after a number, or before the margin (*give or take a few minutes*)

senses.gloss: Approximately; perhaps a little more or less.
examples: The drive takes three hours, *give or take*.
There were 200 people there, *give or take* a few.
It'll cost about $500, *give or take* fifty dollars.

contrast: Informal American. It is not *good* plus *and*: *I'll leave when I'm good and ready* means *when I'm completely ready, not before*.

senses.gloss: Very; completely.
examples: I'll leave when I'm *good and* ready.
By the time the pizza came, we were *good and* hungry.
Let the pan get *good and* hot before you add the oil.

ru: во всём (прислуживать); по рукам и ногам
type: manner — attending to every need; also tied by hands and feet

senses.gloss: Taking care of every need, as a servant would.
examples: He expects his wife to wait on him *hand and foot*.
The hotel staff waited on the guests *hand and foot*.

senses.gloss: With both the hands and the feet tied.
examples: The robbers left the clerk tied *hand and foot*.
The hostages were bound *hand and foot*.

type: manner — in very close cooperation, often for something shady

senses.gloss: In very close cooperation, often in a secret or dishonest way.
examples: The police were accused of working *hand in glove* with the gangs.
The marketing team works *hand in glove* with sales.
The two companies operated *hand in glove* to fix prices.

ru: взявшись за руки; рука об руку
type: manner — holding hands; also closely connected

senses.gloss: Holding each other's hand.
examples: The couple walked *hand in hand* along the beach.
Two little girls skipped *hand in hand* down the sidewalk.

senses.gloss: Closely connected, so that one comes with the other.
examples: Poverty and poor health often go *hand in hand*.
Freedom and responsibility go *hand in hand*.

type: degree — very fast and in large amounts
modifies: verbs of gaining or losing money: *make*, *lose*, *earn*

senses.gloss: Very quickly and in large amounts, usually about money.
examples: The new app is making money *hand over fist*.
The airline was losing money *hand over fist*.
During the boom, real estate agents earned cash *hand over fist*.

ru: впроголодь, еле сводя концы с концами
type: manner — with only just enough money to survive
contrast: Hyphenated before a noun: *a hand-to-mouth existence*.

senses.gloss: With just enough money for immediate needs and nothing saved.
senses.ru: впроголодь, еле сводя концы с концами
examples: After he lost his job, the family lived *hand to mouth*.
Many young artists live *hand to mouth* for years.
We were getting by *hand to mouth* on one small paycheck.

position: end — also before a superlative (*hands down the best*)

senses.gloss: Easily and without any doubt.
examples: Our team won the game *hands down*.
This is *hands down* the best pizza in town.
She beat the other candidates *hands down*.

position: end — after *be* or *stand*, followed by what is surpassed
modifies: verbs such as *be*, *stand*, *rise*, with a noun after *above*
contrast: Russian says *на голову выше*; English needs both parts: *head and shoulders above*.

senses.gloss: Much better than others.
examples: Her essay was *head and shoulders above* the rest.
As a leader, he stands *head and shoulders above* his rivals.
This phone is *head and shoulders above* last year's model.

type: degree — completely, of being in love; also manner: tumbling

senses.gloss: Completely, especially of being in love.
examples: He fell *head over heels* in love with her.
They're *head over heels* for each other.

senses.gloss: Turning over and over.
examples: She tripped and tumbled *head over heels* down the hill.
The skier went *head over heels* into the snow.

modifies: verbs, especially *throw yourself into*, *believe*, *give yourself to*
contrast: Also a noun phrase: *put your heart and soul into something* (вложить душу).

senses.gloss: With all of one's energy and feeling.
examples: She threw herself *heart and soul* into the campaign.
He believed *heart and soul* in the cause.
The coach gave himself *heart and soul* to the team.

modifies: verbs; also after a noun (*a few clouds here and there*)

senses.gloss: In a few different places.
examples: There were a few clouds *here and there*.
I've made a few changes *here and there*.
Toys were scattered *here and there* across the floor.

senses.gloss: Everywhere, when searching for something.
examples: We searched *high and low* for my keys.
I looked *high and low* but couldn't find the receipt.
They hunted *high and low* for a good babysitter.

type: degree — completely, of believing a lie or trick
form: fishing image: the fish swallows the hook, the line and the lead weight

senses.gloss: Completely, without any doubt, about believing something false.
examples: I told him I was a doctor, and he believed it *hook, line, and sinker*.
The investors fell for the scam *hook, line, and sinker*.
She swallowed his excuse *hook, line, and sinker*.

type: degree — points to something bigger or stronger that may be true
position: before its word — between two words or amounts: *hundreds, if not thousands*
modifies: numbers, adjectives and noun phrases, the second stronger than the first
contrast: It usually raises the claim: *hundreds, if not thousands* = сотни, а то и тысячи. It can be ambiguous in writing: *a difficult, if not impossible, task* raises the claim, but *an interesting, if not original, idea* can mean *though not original*. At the start of a clause (*If not, call me*) it is just *if* + *not*, meaning *otherwise*.

senses.gloss: Possibly even; used before a stronger word or a bigger amount.
examples: The repairs will take weeks, *if not* months.
She is one of the best players, *if not* the best, in the league.
Hundreds, *if not* thousands, of people lined the streets.

senses.gloss: Very quickly; almost immediately.
examples: I'll be back *in a flash*.
The waiter was at our table *in a flash*.
*In a flash*, the thief grabbed her bag and ran.

senses.gloss: In very few words; briefly.
examples: *In a nutshell*, we need more money.
That's the whole story *in a nutshell*.
So, *in a nutshell*, the project is two months behind.

contrast: *In a way* (в каком-то смысле) is not *in the way* (мешать, загораживать: *Your bag is in the way*) or *on the way* (по пути).

senses.gloss: To some extent; in some respects.
examples: *In a way*, I'm glad it happened.
He's right, *in a way*.
The ending was sad but, *in a way*, hopeful.

contrast: Followed by *of* it becomes a preposition: *in advance of the meeting* (до встречи).

senses.gloss: Before a particular time or event.
examples: Please buy your tickets *in advance*.
Thanks *in advance* for your help.
The landlord asked us to pay a month *in advance*.

modifies: a clause with a number or amount
contrast: *In all* (всего) is not *at all* (вообще, совсем): *There were 30 people in all* vs *I didn't like it at all*.

senses.gloss: In total.
examples: *In all*, more than 500 people attended.
The trip cost about $2,000 *in all*.
We visited six countries *in all*.

senses.gloss: Very probably.
examples: *In all likelihood*, the flight will be delayed.
He will, *in all likelihood*, be the next mayor.
The painting is *in all likelihood* a fake.

senses.gloss: Very probably.
examples: *In all probability*, the storm will miss the coast.
The bill will, *in all probability*, pass the Senate.
Prices will *in all probability* keep rising.

position: after its word — right after the noun it limits; also end
modifies: a noun or a whole statement

senses.gloss: Considered alone, without anything else.
examples: Money, *in and of itself*, won't make you happy.
The idea isn't bad *in and of itself*.
Being late once is not a problem *in and of itself*.

ru: в любом случае; да и вообще
type: linking — whatever happens; also adds a stronger reason

senses.gloss: Whatever happens or happened; regardless.
examples: It might rain, but we're going *in any case*.
*In any case*, I'll call you when I land.

senses.gloss: Besides; used to add a stronger reason or return to the main point.
senses.ru: да и вообще, как бы то ни было
examples: I can't afford that car, and *in any case* I don't need one.
I'm not sure what happened. *In any case*, it's over now.

ru: в любом случае, так или иначе

senses.gloss: Whatever happens or has happened.
senses.ru: в любом случае, так или иначе
examples: *In any event*, the decision is final.
The meeting may be canceled, but we'll send the report *in any event*.
I don't know if he saw the email; *in any event*, he didn't reply.

position: front or end — also mid between commas

senses.gloss: In a few words; briefly.
examples: *In brief*, the company is doing well.
Here is the news *in brief*.
The report, *in brief*, recommends closing two stores.

type: manner — all together at the same time

senses.gloss: All together, at the same time.
examples: 'Good morning!' the children said *in chorus*.
The fans chanted his name *in chorus*.
Critics complained *in chorus* about the new tax.

type: manner — around and around, often getting nowhere

senses.gloss: Around and around; figuratively, without making any progress.
examples: The hawk flew *in circles* above the field.
We've been going around *in circles* on this issue for weeks.
He talks *in circles* and never answers the question.

senses.gloss: Deliberately and without feeling or pity.
examples: The victims were shot *in cold blood*.
He murdered his business partner *in cold blood*.
The soldiers killed the prisoners *in cold blood*.

contrast: Russian *у нас много общего* becomes *We have a lot in common*, not *We have a lot of common*. *Common* alone is an adjective meaning *usual* (обычный).

senses.gloss: Shared by two or more people or things.
examples: My sister and I have nothing *in common*.
What do these three cases have *in common*?
We had a love of jazz *in common*.

contrast: It can also mean *performing live* (*Springsteen in concert*); the adverb means *together*.

senses.gloss: Together, in agreement or cooperation.
examples: The two agencies acted *in concert* to stop the fraud.
Central banks moved *in concert* to cut interest rates.
The muscles work *in concert* to move the arm.

senses.gloss: As a final point; to finish.
examples: *In conclusion*, I'd like to thank our sponsors.
*In conclusion*, the evidence supports the new policy.
And so, *in conclusion*, we recommend a second study.

type: manner — thoroughly, with all the facts
contrast: Singular: *in detail*, not *in details*. *In more detail* and *in great detail* are common.

senses.gloss: Thoroughly, including all the facts.
examples: The doctor explained the procedure *in detail*.
We'll discuss the budget *in more detail* next week.
She described the attacker *in great detail*.

type: time — at the proper time, eventually

senses.gloss: At the appropriate time; eventually.
examples: You will receive your results *in due course*.
*In due course*, the truth came out.
The details will be announced *in due course*.

senses.gloss: Seriously and with full effort; to a real degree.
examples: The cleanup began *in earnest* the next morning.
Once the rain started *in earnest*, everyone ran inside.
He's been studying *in earnest* since he failed the first exam.

type: viewpoint — in actual fact, in practice
contrast: After *be*, *remain* or *go into*, *in effect* means *in force* (в силе, действует): *The law is in effect*. That use is predicative, not this adverb.

senses.gloss: In practice, even if not in name.
examples: *In effect*, the new rule bans smoking everywhere downtown.
His silence was, *in effect*, an admission of guilt.
By cutting the budget, they *in effect* closed the program.

senses.gloss: Basically; in its most important nature.
examples: *In essence*, the two plans are the same.
What he said was, *in essence*, 'no.'
The job is *in essence* customer service.

type: stance — really, actually; also linking: adds a stronger point
contrast: False friend: Russian *фактически* often means *practically, virtually*, which is *in effect* or *virtually* in English. *In fact* means *really* or *more than that*.

senses.gloss: In reality, contrary to what might be expected.
examples: Everyone thought she was angry, but *in fact* she was relieved.
The plant looks dead, but *in fact* it's just dormant.

senses.gloss: Used to add a stronger or more exact point.
examples: I like the city. *In fact*, I'm thinking of moving there.
It was cold; *in fact*, it was the coldest day of the year.

contrast: Without *of* it is an adverb: *Let's sit in front*. With *of* it is a preposition: *in front of the house*. It does not mean *напротив* (on the other side of a street); that is *across from*: *The bank is across from the hotel*.

senses.gloss: In a position ahead or at the front.
examples: Let's sit *in front* so we can see the screen.
By the tenth mile she was far *in front*.
The house has a small garden *in front*.

senses.gloss: Completely; the whole amount or text.
examples: The loan must be paid *in full* by June.
Please write your name *in full*.
The newspaper printed the letter *in full*.

type: time — at the busiest, most active stage

senses.gloss: At the most active or lively stage.
examples: By ten o'clock the party was *in full swing*.
Holiday shopping is *in full swing*.
When we arrived, the game was already *in full swing*.

position: front or end — also right after a noun (*people in general*)
contrast: *In general* (в целом) is not *in common* (общего): *We have a lot in common*. After a noun it means *as a whole*: *teenagers in general*.

senses.gloss: Usually; considering the whole rather than details.
examples: *In general*, the weather here is mild.
I like his movies *in general*, but this one was boring.
Americans *in general* are eating less red meat.

contrast: Three look-alikes: *in hand* = under control (*The situation is in hand*); *on hand* = available, nearby (под рукой: *Keep some cash on hand*); *at hand* = close in time or place (*Help is at hand*).

senses.gloss: Under control; being dealt with.
examples: Don't worry, the police have the situation *in hand*.
Preparations for the wedding are well *in hand*.
The new coach quickly took the struggling team *in hand*.

type: manner — in the same way; also in goods rather than money
contrast: Before a noun it is a hyphenated adjective: *in-kind donations*. It has nothing to do with *kind* (добрый).

senses.gloss: In the same way as one was treated.
examples: When he insulted her, she answered *in kind*.
The other team played rough, so we responded *in kind*.

senses.gloss: With goods or services instead of money.
examples: Farmers sometimes paid their rent *in kind*, with grain.
The company contributed *in kind*, supplying computers instead of cash.

type: place — in a queue; also manner: under control
contrast: Americans *wait in line*; the British *queue*. *In line with* (в соответствии с) is a preposition: *in line with the rules*.

senses.gloss: In a row of people waiting their turn.
examples: We waited *in line* for two hours to get tickets.
Please stand *in line* until your number is called.

senses.gloss: Under control; obeying the rules.
examples: The new coach keeps his players *in line*.
One warning was enough to bring him back *in line*.
